You are jolly_ember22, one of 10 agents working together on the same task on a shared platform. All
10 agents form one group, and you work with brisk_harbor75, early_island22, gentle_otter27, pale_kettle84, pale_lantern48, rapid_thistle87, sandy_walnut42, urban_comet97, zesty_lantern63. Each agent works in its own sandbox, on its
own git repository. Your group shares one `main` branch, which every member can push to, and one channel
(`group`). Work together with your teammates to make your group's `main` as good as possible. Use `group` to
coordinate and share helpful findings.

## Setting
Your task is to recreate a program from scratch based only on its observable behavior and bundled documentation.
You are given a reference executable and its documentation.
Treat the reference executable as a specification you can query through its normal user interface.

Your submission must be an independent implementation.
Using the original source code, wrapping the reference executable, or installing an existing implementation does not satisfy the task and will receive no credit.
It will be detected by an automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.

<RULES>
## What is NOT allowed

### 1. Using an existing implementation

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the reference executable

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The reference `/opt/reference/executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the reference executable (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that only runs `chmod +x ./executable` or copies the reference executable (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. How the reference executable may be observed

All information about the reference `/opt/reference/executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `/opt/reference/executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `/opt/reference/executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the reference `/opt/reference/executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

## Your repository and your group's main
- In your sandbox, `/workspace` is your own git repository, and the reference executable is in `/opt/reference`. No one else can see it.
- Your group's shared `main` is the remote `team`. Fetch it with `git fetch team` (you get `team/main`),
  and push to it with `git push team HEAD:main`. **Your local files do not update automatically when a
  teammate pushes.**
- A push must be a fast-forward: if `main` has moved since you last fetched, the push is rejected. Fetch,
  merge `team/main` into your work, and push again.
- When you push, the platform posts in `group` on your behalf, with your commit message, a summary of the
  changed files, and a pointer to the new `main`. Write commit messages that say what changed.
- Your git name and email are preconfigured as your agent name. Do not change them.
- Commit with `git commit -m "<message>"`: there is no editor in the sandbox, so a commit without `-m`
  fails with an empty message.
- Run the reference executable and your experiments outside `/workspace` (for example in `/tmp`), so that they do not change your
  repository.

## Scoring rule
Your payoff is your group's final score: the fraction of hidden tests passed by the code on `main` at
the end. Every agent receives the same payoff.
- **Only the code on your group's `main` at the end is graded.** Code in your own repository, or shared
  through pointers, does not count until it is pushed to `main`. If no one pushes, the initial commit is
  graded.
- Everyone keeps working until time runs out.

## Platform
The platform is the shared place where agents announce what they are exploring, building, or have found,
and ask each other questions. Typical posts include a direction you are exploring, a component you are
building, a finding (how the original program behaves in some case, a useful test command, a tricky edge case), a proposal for how to organize the work, or a question.
- `post` publishes a message to `group`, with a title: a one-line summary of the message, up
  to 120 characters. Every post gets a number. Mention someone with @name.
- To share code, commit it, then list it in the post's `attach`. The platform adds a pointer
  (`[[<sha>:<path>#La-b]]`) to the post for each item. `attach` can name:
  - `path#La-b`: a file in your `HEAD`, optionally with a line range;
  - `<sha>:path#La-b`: a file in another commit;
  - a commit's sha, or `HEAD`: a whole commit;
  - `file:<path>#La-b`: the current content of a single file, even if it is not committed. Readers see
    only that file.
  Pointing at a commit makes all files in that commit readable. Uncommitted changes are not shared.
- `read_feed` lists the new posts in `group`, and any unopened posts that mention you, one line each
  (number, author, channel, title). `read_feed` with a post's number shows its full text, with its
  pointers expanded into the code and a diff against your own version.
- You can fetch any code shared with you into your repository with `git fetch origin` (as
  `origin/shared/<author>/<sha>`), and then merge or cherry-pick what you want.

After each action, a platform notice lists the new posts on the channels you can read, one line each (number,
author, channel, title, and a marker when the post carries code). A post that mentions you appears in
every notice until you open it with `read_feed` and its number.

## Working together
- Start by **getting an overview of what the reference program supports**, enough to understand how the
  program should behave in its main cases, and share it in `group` as a list (if a teammate has
  already posted one, add to theirs), so the group can keep extending the plan and everyone stays up
  to date on which areas are covered. Then **agree with your teammates on how to work together**:
  split the work, or have several members build the same part and compare, keeping the best of each.
  If parts depend on each other, agree on the interfaces first, and while you wait for a part you
  need, write tests for it with expected output from the reference program.
- If a teammate has already posted a plan, **follow it and propose changes to it** instead of posting
  a competing one.
- Work in a cycle: (1) pick an area and say so in `group`; (2) build it on top of the latest `main`;
  (3) compare its output with the reference program on the same inputs; (4) commit, `git fetch team`, merge
  `team/main`, and `git push team HEAD:main`; (5) post what you finished, with a pointer, then go back
  to (1). Report a part as done only once it is on `main`: a part that is not on `main` does not count.
- Passing your own tests does not mean the task is done: always assume the hidden tests cover more
  than your tests do. **When your tests all pass, test more areas.** Add cases for features and
  options your tests do not cover yet, including the parts your teammates are handling. A new area
  usually matters more than more cases in an area that already works.
- **Never stop calling tool before time is up. When you are not sure what to do next, review the
  whole program on `main` again** as a reviewer looking for bugs: features of the reference program that
  are missing or only partly handled, edge cases (empty input, `null`, deep nesting, large numbers,
  unusual option combinations), and error paths. Do not review only your own part: test the whole
  program, including your teammates' parts, with inputs you have not tried yet. Test each suspicion
  against the reference program, and fix what differs.
- **If one approach keeps failing, change the approach instead of retrying it.** Post in `group` what
  you tried, so teammates do not repeat it and can suggest other ideas. If you are still stuck, put a
  version that handles the common cases on `main` for now, and come back to it later.
- Do not leave hard parts as known gaps. Come back to them, discuss them with your teammates, and solve as
  many of them as possible: **keep improving `main` until time runs out.**

# Dasel Dasel (short for **Data-Select**) is a command-line tool and library for querying, modifying, and transforming data structures such as JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, and KDL. It provides a consistent, powerful syntax to traverse and update data — making it useful for developers, DevOps, and data wrangling tasks. --- ## Features * **Multi-format support**: JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, HCL, INI, KDL. * **Unified query syntax**: Access data in any format with the same selectors. * **Query & search**: Extract values, lists, or structures with intuitive syntax. * **Modify in place**: Update, insert, or delete values directly in structured files. * **Convert between formats**: Seamlessly transform data from JSON → YAML, TOML → JSON, etc. * **Script-friendly**: Simple CLI integration for shell scripts and pipelines. * **Library support**: Import and use in Go projects. --- ## Installation ### Homebrew (macOS/Linux) ```sh brew install dasel ``` ### Go Install ```sh go install github.com/tomwright/dasel/v3/cmd/dasel@master ``` ### Prebuilt Binaries Prebuilt binaries are available on the [Releases](https://github.com/TomWright/dasel/releases) page for Linux, macOS, and Windows. ### None of the above? See the [installation docs](https://daseldocs.tomwright.me/getting-started/installation) for more options. --- ## Shell Completion Dasel supports tab-completion for Bash, Zsh, Fish, and PowerShell. Generate and load the completion script for your shell: ```sh # Bash source <(dasel completion bash) # Zsh source <(dasel completion zsh) # Fish dasel completion fish | source # PowerShell dasel completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression ``` See the [shell completion docs](https://daseldocs.tomwright.me/getting-started/shell-completion) for permanent installation instructions. ## Man Page Generate and view the man page: ```sh dasel man | man -l - ``` --- ## Basic Usage ### Selecting Values By default, Dasel evaluates the final selector and prints the result. ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json 'foo.bar' # Output: "baz" ``` ### Modifying Values Update values inline: ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json 'foo.bar = "bong"' # Output: "bong" ``` Use `--root` to output the full document after modification: ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json --root 'foo.bar = "bong"' # Output: { "foo": { "bar": "bong" } } ``` Update values based on previous value: ```sh echo '[1,2,3,4,5]' | dasel -i json --root 'each($this = $this*2)' # Output: [ 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 ] ``` ### Format Conversion ```sh cat data.json | dasel -i json -o yaml ``` ### Recursive Descent (`..`) Searches all nested objects and arrays for a matching key or index. ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json '..bar' # Output: [ "baz" ] ``` ### Search (`search`) Finds all values matching a condition anywhere in the structure. ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json 'search(bar == "baz")' # Output: [ { "bar": "baz" } ] ``` --- ## Documentation Full documentation is available at [daseldocs.tomwright.me](https://daseldocs.tomwright.me). --- ## Contributing Contributions are welcome! Please see the [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) for details. --- ## License MIT License. See [LICENSE](./LICENSE) for details. ## Stargazers over time [![Stargazers over time](https://starchart.cc/TomWright/dasel.svg)](https://starchart.cc/TomWright/dasel) # Model The model package contains the Value struct and functionality for the application. `model.Value` is just a wrapper around `reflect.Value` but provides some additional logic for easier use. # Selector The selector package contains everything needed to parse a selector string into an AST, which we can then execute. # Execution The execution package accepts a `model.Value`, parses a selector and executes the resulting AST on the value. const patch = "*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /workspace/ini_format.py
+"""Small INI adapter for the Dasel CLI compatibility layer."""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+
+def parse_ini(text: str) -> dict:
+    """Parse INI into nested dictionaries, keeping all values as strings."""
+    result: dict = {}
+    section: dict = result
+    for raw in text.splitlines():
+        line = raw.strip()
+        if not line or line.startswith((";", "#")):
+            continue
+        if line.startswith("[") and line.endswith("]"):
+            name = line[1:-1].strip()
+            section = result.setdefault(name, {})
+            if not isinstance(section, dict):
+                section = {}
+                result[name] = section
+            continue
+        # Inline comments are data in INI values, so only whole-line comments
+        # are stripped.
+        if "=" in line:
+            key, value = line.split("=", 1)
+        elif ":" in line:
+            key, value = line.split(":", 1)
+        else:
+            key, value = line, ""
+        section[key.strip()] = value.strip()
+    return result
+
+
+def dump_ini(value) -> str:
+    """Serialize a map using the simple section/key syntax accepted by Dasel."""
+    if not isinstance(value, dict):
+        raise ValueError("ini can only represent map values")
+    lines: list[str] = []
+    root_items = [(k, v) for k, v in value.items() if not isinstance(v, dict)]
+    if any(not isinstance(v, dict) for v in value.values()):
+        if any(isinstance(v, dict) for v in value.values()):
+            # INI represents root keys as the unnamed/default section.
+            lines.extend(f"{k} = {_scalar(v)}" for k, v in root_items)
+            lines.append("")
+        else:
+            lines.extend(f"{k} = {_scalar(v)}" for k, v in value.items())
+    for key, section in value.items():
+        if not isinstance(section, dict):
+            continue
+        if lines and lines[-1] != "":
+            lines.append("")
+        lines.append(f"[{key}]")
+        lines.extend(f"{k} = {_scalar(v)}" for k, v in section.items())
+    return "\n".join(lines) + ("\n" if lines else "")
+
+
+def _scalar(value) -> str:
+    if isinstance(value, (dict, list)):
+        raise ValueError("ini can only represent map values")
+    if value is None:
+        return ""
+    if value is True:
+        return "true"
+    if value is False:
+        return "false"
+    return str(value)
*** End Patch";
text(await tools.apply_patch(patch));

+                text=raw.lstrip()
+                container='array' if text.startswith('[') else 'object' if text.startswith('{') else None
+                detail=e.msg
+                if e.msg.startswith('Expecting property name') and e.pos<len(raw):
+                    detail=f'json: invalid character {raw[e.pos]} as token'
+                elif e.msg.startswith('Expecting value') and text:
+                    token=text
+                    if token.startswith('n') and token != 'null':
+                        idx=next((i for i,(a,b) in enumerate(zip(token,'null')) if a!=b),min(len(token),3))
+                        detail=f'json: invalid character {token[idx]} as null'
+                    elif token.startswith('f') and token != 'false':
+                        idx=next((i for i,(a,b) in enumerate(zip(token,'false')) if a!=b),min(len(token),4))
+                        detail=f'json: invalid character {token[idx]} as bool(false)'
+                    elif token.startswith('t') and token != 'true':
+                        idx=next((i for i,(a,b) in enumerate(zip(token,'true')) if a!=b),min(len(token),3))
+                        detail=f'json: invalid character {token[idx]} as bool(true)'
+                    elif token[0] not in 'ntf':
+                        detail=f'json: invalid character {token[0]} as token'
+                elif e.pos<len(raw) and raw[e.pos:e.pos+1]:
+                    char=raw[e.pos]
+                    if char not in ' \r\n\t,:}]': detail=f'json: invalid character {char} as token'
+                if container: detail=f'could not decode {container}: {detail}'
                 print(f'dasel: error: error reading input: {detail}',file=sys.stderr)

## Current task

Reimplement the reference CLI in Python 3.10 using only bundled documentation and reference behavior. Work in `/workspace`; the shared submission is `team/main`. Do not run `compile.sh` or use external implementations. Keep reviewing and pushing useful fixes; the user explicitly asked not to stop tool use before time runs out.

## Progress

The implementation covers the query CLI, common selectors and functions, YAML/TOML/INI/CSV/XML/KDL/HCL formats, auxiliary commands, variables, and format flags. I contributed and pushed INI support, XML mixed-content behavior, variable expressions, writer/input error reporting, typed comparisons, quoted bracket keys, and chained ranges on array literals. These changes are on shared `main`.

Latest local state after fetching and merging was `370c7c6`; the shared branch may have moved since. Check with `git fetch team` before editing or pushing.

## Active issue to investigate first

A recent differential check found the latest `main` fails reference-supported permissive JSON inputs. For example, the reference accepts `[1,,2]`, `[,1]`, `[1 2]`, `[true false null]`, `{"a":1 "b":2}`, `{,"a":1}`, and `{"a" 1}`. Current `main.py` imports `parse_json` from `json_input.py`, but the local `json_input.py` still uses strict `json.loads`; all these cases errored in the implementation.

Agent zesty_lantern63 shared a draft tolerant decoder in post #315, pointer commit `ba8a94ac7c0a:json_input.py`. Agent brisk_thistle87 confirmed additional reference cases in post #316. Inspect or fetch that draft, compare it with the current `json_input.py`, then integrate, manually compare outputs, and push. Preserve the existing int64 range and malformed-input diagnostic behavior.

## Recent observations

- Filters must reject comparisons between distinct types, including `false == 0`; integer and float comparisons are compatible. Error context should match the reference.
- `&&`/`||` work in filter expressions; textual `and`/`or` are rejected by the reference.
- Quoted selector keys containing `]` now parse correctly; e.g. `a["a]b"]`.
- `[1][0:0]` returns `[1]`; chained ranges on array literals were added.
- XML mixed content concatenates child tails and emits `#text` before child keys.
- Default output format follows the input format. INI values parse as strings; nested INI output uses sections like `[a]` and `[a b]`.

## Next steps

1. Fetch `team/main` and inspect current `json_input.py` plus the shared tolerant decoder draft.
2. Integrate and compare the permissive JSON cases above against `/opt/reference/executable`.
3. Check for new group posts and avoid duplicating active work.
4. Continue differential review of the integrated CLI; commit, fetch/merge, and push every useful fix to `team/main`.

I’ll resume from the current shared branch, check the unread XML findings, and focus first on the permissive JSON discrepancy from the handoff. Then I’ll run fresh reference comparisons and push any verified fix.

"""JSON decoding rules for Dasel's int64-backed JSON values."""
import json


class JsonIntegerRangeError(ValueError):
    pass


def _parse_int(token):
    value = int(token)
    if value < -(1 << 63) or value > (1 << 63) - 1:
        raise JsonIntegerRangeError(token)
    return value


def loads(text):
    # The reference decoder tokenizes container values permissively: commas
    # may be repeated or omitted between otherwise complete members.
    decoder = json.JSONDecoder(parse_int=_parse_int)
    pos = 0

    def ws(i):
        while i < len(text) and (text[i].isspace() or text[i] == ','):
            i += 1
        return i

    def value(i):
        i = ws(i)
        if i >= len(text): raise ValueError('unexpected end')
        if text[i] == '[':
            out=[]; i+=1
            while True:
                i=ws(i)
                if i>=len(text): raise ValueError('unexpected end')
                if text[i]==']': return out,i+1
                item,i=value(i); out.append(item)
        if text[i] == '{':
            out={}; i+=1
            while True:
                i=ws(i)
                if i>=len(text): raise ValueError('unexpected end')
                if text[i]=='}': return out,i+1
                key,end=decoder.raw_decode(text,i)
                if not isinstance(key,str): raise ValueError('object key is not string')
                i=ws(end)
                if i>=len(text) or text[i]!=':': raise ValueError('missing colon')
                item,i=value(i+1); out[key]=item
        return decoder.raw_decode(text,i)

    try:
        result,end=value(0)
        if ws(end)==len(text): return result
    except (ValueError, json.JSONDecodeError):
        pass
    try:
        return json.loads(text, parse_int=_parse_int)
    except JsonIntegerRangeError as exc:
        token = str(exc)
        stripped = text.lstrip()
        kind = 'object' if stripped.startswith('{') else 'array' if stripped.startswith('[') else None
        middle = f'could not decode {kind}: ' if kind else ''
        raise ValueError(f'error reading input: {middle}strconv.ParseInt: parsing "{token}": value out of range') from None

# Dasel Dasel (short for **Data-Select**) is a command-line tool and library for querying, modifying, and transforming data structures such as JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, and KDL. It provides a consistent, powerful syntax to traverse and update data — making it useful for developers, DevOps, and data wrangling tasks. --- ## Features * **Multi-format support**: JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, CSV, HCL, INI, KDL. * **Unified query syntax**: Access data in any format with the same selectors. * **Query & search**: Extract values, lists, or structures with intuitive syntax. * **Modify in place**: Update, insert, or delete values directly in structured files. * **Convert between formats**: Seamlessly transform data from JSON → YAML, TOML → JSON, etc. * **Script-friendly**: Simple CLI integration for shell scripts and pipelines. * **Library support**: Import and use in Go projects. --- ## Installation ### Homebrew (macOS/Linux) ```sh brew install dasel ``` ### Go Install ```sh go install github.com/tomwright/dasel/v3/cmd/dasel@master ``` ### Prebuilt Binaries Prebuilt binaries are available on the [Releases](https://github.com/TomWright/dasel/releases) page for Linux, macOS, and Windows. ### None of the above? See the [installation docs](https://daseldocs.tomwright.me/getting-started/installation) for more options. --- ## Shell Completion Dasel supports tab-completion for Bash, Zsh, Fish, and PowerShell. Generate and load the completion script for your shell: ```sh # Bash source <(dasel completion bash) # Zsh source <(dasel completion zsh) # Fish dasel completion fish | source # PowerShell dasel completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression ``` See the [shell completion docs](https://daseldocs.tomwright.me/getting-started/shell-completion) for permanent installation instructions. ## Man Page Generate and view the man page: ```sh dasel man | man -l - ``` --- ## Basic Usage ### Selecting Values By default, Dasel evaluates the final selector and prints the result. ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json 'foo.bar' # Output: "baz" ``` ### Modifying Values Update values inline: ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json 'foo.bar = "bong"' # Output: "bong" ``` Use `--root` to output the full document after modification: ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json --root 'foo.bar = "bong"' # Output: { "foo": { "bar": "bong" } } ``` Update values based on previous value: ```sh echo '[1,2,3,4,5]' | dasel -i json --root 'each($this = $this*2)' # Output: [ 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 ] ``` ### Format Conversion ```sh cat data.json | dasel -i json -o yaml ``` ### Recursive Descent (`..`) Searches all nested objects and arrays for a matching key or index. ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json '..bar' # Output: [ "baz" ] ``` ### Search (`search`) Finds all values matching a condition anywhere in the structure. ```sh echo '{"foo": {"bar": "baz"}}' | dasel -i json 'search(bar == "baz")' # Output: [ { "bar": "baz" } ] ``` --- ## Documentation Full documentation is available at [daseldocs.tomwright.me](https://daseldocs.tomwright.me). --- ## Contributing Contributions are welcome!
